topics.name: Electrolytes
topics.kicker: Conduct electricity when dissolved or melted · They break apart into ions
topics.briefing: An electrolyte is any substance that breaks apart into ions when it dissolves in water or melts, so the liquid can carry an electric current. Table salt is a strong electrolyte, the acid in vinegar is a weak one, and sugar is not one at all. Your nerves and muscles depend on electrolytes like sodium and potassium ions, which is why sports drinks advertise them, and every battery needs one between its two electrodes.
topics.answerHtml: Electrolytes (accept electrolyte; accept strong or weak electrolytes; prompt on ionic compounds; do not accept “electrolysis”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Svante Arrhenius’s 1884 doctoral thesis on these substances earned only a low grade at Uppsala, but his theory of how they dissociate in water later won him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. That theory explained why their solutions freeze at lower temperatures than expected.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, like table salt, that conduct electricity when dissolved in water because they release ions.

tossups.p: In 1834, Michael Faraday introduced this term along with the words electrode, anode, and cathode. Its name comes partly from a Greek root meaning “loosened,” because Faraday saw these substances break apart when a current passes through them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as salt or acids, whose solutions conduct electricity because they contain ions.

tossups.p: The van ’t Hoff [“vahnt HOFF”] factor of a strong one of these substances is about equal to the number of ions in its formula, about 2 for sodium chloride and about 3 for calcium chloride. That is why they lower water’s freezing point more than the same number of sugar molecules would.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as sodium chloride, that conduct electricity when dissolved because they split into ions.

tossups.p: A basic blood test checks the levels of several of these substances, including sodium, potassium, and chloride. In a classic lemon battery, the fruit’s acidic juice serves as one of these substances, letting ions carry charge between strips of zinc and copper pushed into the lemon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, like table salt, that conduct electricity in water because they release ions.

tossups.p: Debye–Hückel [“duh-BYE HUE-kul”] theory, published in 1923, explains why dilute solutions of these substances behave less than ideally: each ion is surrounded by a loose cloud of oppositely charged ions that partly shields it. That theory calculates the activity coefficients of their ions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as sodium chloride, whose solutions conduct electricity because they contain ions.

tossups.p: Wilhelm Ostwald’s [“OST-vahlts”] dilution law describes how weak examples of these substances break apart into ions more completely as their solutions are diluted. Weak examples include acetic acid and ammonia, while strong examples, like hydrochloric acid, break apart completely.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, like table salt, that conduct electricity when dissolved in water.

tossups.p: When the two wires of a conductivity tester are dipped into solutions, its bulb glows brightly for strong examples of these substances, glows dimly for weak ones such as the acid in vinegar, and stays dark for sugar water. Solid ionic compounds do not conduct, because their ions cannot move until they are melted or dissolved.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as salts, acids, and bases, that conduct electricity in water because they break apart into ions.

tossups.p: Car batteries use sulfuric acid as this kind of substance, alkaline batteries use potassium hydroxide, and lithium-ion batteries use a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent. Solid-state batteries replace that liquid with a solid that still lets ions move.
tossups.r: Every battery needs one of these between its two electrodes. For 10 points, name these substances that conduct electricity by letting ions move.

tossups.p: In a galvanic cell, a salt bridge filled with a solution of one of these substances, such as potassium nitrate, lets ions flow between the two half-cells so the circuit stays complete. Without that bridge, charge would build up and the current would quickly stop.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as table salt, whose solutions conduct electricity because they contain ions.

tossups.p: The hormone aldosterone [“al-DOSS-tuh-rone”] tells the kidneys to hold on to sodium, one of these substances in the blood, and doctors call a low level of sodium in the blood hyponatremia [“hy-poh-nuh-TREE-mee-uh”]. The kidneys keep the body’s levels of these substances steady.
tossups.r: Gatorade was invented in 1965 to replace the water and these substances lost in sweat. For 10 points, name these substances, which sports drinks advertise.

tossups.p: Oral rehydration solution, a simple mix of clean water, salt, and sugar, replaces the water and these substances lost to diarrhea and has saved millions of lives from diseases like cholera. The sugar in it helps the intestine absorb sodium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as sodium and potassium ions, that sports drinks also replace.

tossups.p: In a Downs cell, molten sodium chloride serves as this kind of substance, and electricity splits it into sodium metal and chlorine gas. Calcium chloride is mixed in to lower the melting point, which saves energy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances that conduct electricity when melted or dissolved in water, because their ions can move.

tossups.p: Many hydrogen fuel cells use a plastic membrane such as Nafion as this kind of substance, because it lets protons pass through but blocks electrons. Distilled water barely conducts, so chemists dissolve a little of one of these substances, such as sulfuric acid, in water before splitting it with an electric current.
tossups.r: Seawater conducts electricity far better than fresh water because it is full of these substances. For 10 points, name these substances, like table salt, that release ions when dissolved.

tossups.p: When one of these substances dissolves, water molecules crowd around each ion, pointing their partly negative oxygen atoms toward positive ions and their partly positive hydrogen atoms toward negative ones. Those surrounding clusters of water are called hydration shells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as sodium chloride, whose solutions conduct electricity because they contain ions.

tossups.p: Oxygen sensors in car exhaust systems use a ceramic called zirconia as a solid version of this kind of substance, because oxide ions can move through it when it is hot. Sugar and ethanol, which dissolve as whole, uncharged molecules, are not examples of these substances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as table salt, that conduct electricity when dissolved because they split into ions.

trap.title: Not electrolysis!
trap.body: Electrolytes and electrolysis share the same Greek root, and clues about batteries, electrodes, and splitting water fit both. But electrolysis is a process that uses an electric current to drive a reaction, while this answer names the substances whose ions carry that current. Ions are the other trap: electrolytes are the substances that release ions, not the charged particles themselves.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these substances” that conduct when dissolved or melted, say electrolytes. If it asks for “this process” that splits compounds with electricity, say electrolysis; if it asks for “these charged particles,” say ions.
trap.line: Real answer line: Electrolytes (accept electrolyte; accept strong or weak electrolytes; prompt on ionic compounds; do not accept “electrolysis”)

topics.name: Haber process
topics.kicker: Ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen · The reaction that feeds billions
topics.briefing: The Haber process turns nitrogen from the air and hydrogen into ammonia, using an iron catalyst, high pressure, and heat. Fritz Haber first made it work in a lab in 1909, and Carl Bosch of the company BASF scaled it up into giant factories. Fertilizer made from that ammonia grows food for billions of people, but the process also let Germany keep making explosives during World War I.
topics.answerHtml: Haber process (or Haber–Bosch process; prompt on Haber alone or on ammonia synthesis)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Gerhard Ertl won the 2007 Nobel Prize in Chemistry partly for showing, step by step, how nitrogen molecules break apart on the iron surface used in this process. The slowest step of this process is splitting nitrogen’s very strong triple bond.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this industrial process that combines nitrogen and hydrogen to make ammonia.

tossups.p: Alwin Mittasch [“MIT-ahsh”] ran thousands of tests to find a cheap catalyst for this process, settling on iron mixed with small amounts of potassium and aluminum oxides. That catalyst replaced the rare metal osmium, used in this process’s first working lab version in 1909.
tossups.r: Most of the product of this process becomes fertilizer. For 10 points, name this process that makes ammonia from nitrogen in the air.

tossups.p: In 1909, the British chemist Robert Le Rossignol [“luh ROSS-in-yol”] helped build the tabletop, high-pressure apparatus that first showed this process working, as its liquid product dripped out drop by drop. That demonstration took place in a lab in Karlsruhe [“KARLS-roo-uh”], Germany.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that combines nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia, using an iron catalyst.

tossups.p: Le Chatelier’s [“luh SHAH-tuh-lyayz”] principle explains why this process runs at about 200 atmospheres: four molecules of gas react to make only two, so high pressure pushes the equilibrium toward the product. Its temperature of about 450 °C is a compromise between yield and speed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that turns nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia over an iron catalyst.

tossups.p: This process answered an 1898 warning from William Crookes that the world would soon run short of the nitrogen compounds needed to grow enough wheat. Before it, farmers depended on seabird droppings called guano and on sodium nitrate, or Chile saltpeter, mined in Chile’s Atacama Desert.
tossups.r: This process solved that problem by turning nitrogen from the air into ammonia. For 10 points, name this industrial process that uses an iron catalyst.

tossups.p: During World War I, a British naval blockade cut Germany off from Chilean saltpeter, but this process let German factories keep making explosives. Its product was burned over platinum in the Ostwald [“OST-vahlt”] process to make nitric acid.
tossups.r: Today, most of its product becomes fertilizer. For 10 points, name this process that makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.

tossups.p: This process soon outcompeted Norway’s Birkeland–Eyde process, which used giant electric arcs to make nitrogen and oxygen combine, because this process needed far less energy. Instead of making nitric oxide, this process makes a different compound using an iron catalyst.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that combines nitrogen with hydrogen to make ammonia, the key ingredient in most fertilizer.

tossups.p: A BASF engineer who scaled this process up shared the 1931 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Friedrich Bergius [“BAIR-gee-us”] for high-pressure methods. That engineer found that hot hydrogen under pressure made ordinary steel brittle, so he designed double-walled reactors with a soft iron lining.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen at high pressure.

tossups.p: The first factory using this process opened in 1913 at Oppau [“OH-pow”], near Ludwigshafen, Germany, and a second, larger plant was built at Leuna [“LOY-nah”] during World War I. The chemical company BASF, which had bought the rights to this process, ran both plants.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that turns nitrogen from the air and hydrogen into ammonia, mostly for fertilizer.

tossups.p: Most of the hydrogen for this process comes from natural gas through steam reforming, which releases large amounts of carbon dioxide. So-called “green” versions of this process instead get hydrogen by splitting water with electricity from wind or solar power.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that combines that hydrogen with nitrogen from the air to make ammonia.

tossups.p: Only part of the gas mixture reacts each time it passes over the catalyst in this process, so the product is removed by cooling it into a liquid, and the unreacted gases are pumped back through again. The reaction is reversible and reaches an equilibrium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen with an iron catalyst.

tossups.p: Scientists estimate that about half of the nitrogen atoms in a typical person’s body have passed through factories that use this process. It has been called the most important invention of the 20th century.
tossups.r: Fertilizer made by this process grows food for billions of people. For 10 points, name this process that turns nitrogen from the air into ammonia.

tossups.p: The inventor of this process won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, but some scientists objected, because he had also directed Germany’s use of chlorine gas as a weapon in World War I. He left Germany in 1933 after the Nazis came to power.
tossups.r: His prize was “for the synthesis of ammonia from its elements.” For 10 points, name this process that makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.

tossups.p: Bacteria in the root nodules of legumes use the enzyme nitrogenase to do at ordinary temperatures what this process needs about 450 °C and 200 atmospheres to do. For that reason, this process is sometimes called industrial nitrogen fixation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen over an iron catalyst.

tossups.p: Sulfur compounds and carbon monoxide must be carefully removed from the gases fed into this process, because they poison its iron catalyst. Catalysts like that iron do not change how much product forms at equilibrium; they only help the reaction get there faster.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this industrial process that combines nitrogen and hydrogen to make ammonia.

trap.title: Process, not product
trap.body: Nearly every clue for this answer also fits ammonia, its product, and nitrogen, its raw material, so players blurt those. Others confuse it with the Ostwald process, which turns ammonia into nitric acid, or with the Born–Haber cycle, an energy calculation for salts like sodium chloride. Saying just “Haber” earns a prompt, so be ready to add “process.”
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this process” or “this reaction,” give the process name; if it asks for “this compound” or “this gas,” say ammonia. Platinum and nitric acid mean the Ostwald process; lattice energy and Hess’s law mean the Born–Haber cycle.
trap.line: Real answer line: Haber process (or Haber–Bosch process; prompt on Haber alone or on ammonia synthesis)

topics.name: Alkenes
topics.kicker: Hydrocarbons with a C=C double bond · Building blocks of plastics
topics.briefing: Alkenes are hydrocarbons with at least one carbon–carbon double bond, and their names end in “-ene,” like ethene and propene. That double bond makes them much more reactive than alkanes: they quickly turn orange bromine water colorless, and they link up by the thousands into plastics such as polyethylene and polypropylene. The simplest one, ethene (also called ethylene), is even a plant hormone that makes fruit ripen.
topics.answerHtml: Alkenes (accept alkene or olefins; prompt on unsaturated hydrocarbons; do not accept “alkanes” or “alkynes”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Yves Chauvin [“shoh-VAN”], Robert Grubbs, and Richard Schrock shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for metathesis, a reaction in which two of these compounds trade carbon groups, like two dancing couples swapping partners. Grubbs’s ruthenium catalysts made that reaction practical in ordinary labs.
tossups.r: These compounds’ names end in “-ene.” For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons that contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond.

tossups.p: A rule named for Vladimir Markovnikov [“mar-KOV-nih-kof”] predicts that when hydrogen bromide adds to one of these compounds, the hydrogen atom goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogen atoms, and the bromine goes to the other carbon.
tossups.r: These compounds turn orange bromine water colorless. For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons with at least one carbon–carbon double bond.

tossups.p: Industrial ethanol can be made by adding steam to the simplest of these compounds over a phosphoric acid catalyst. Olive oil and other unsaturated fats stay liquid at room temperature partly because the bonds that define these compounds put kinks in their fatty-acid chains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons, such as ethene, that have a carbon–carbon double bond.

tossups.p: In ozonolysis [“oh-zoh-NOL-ih-sis”], ozone splits one of these molecules into two pieces, and a reagent such as zinc or dimethyl sulfide then turns those pieces into aldehydes or ketones. Identifying those pieces tells chemists where the original molecule was broken.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons, such as propene, whose carbon–carbon double bonds make them unsaturated.

tossups.p: In Baeyer’s [“BYE-erz”] test, cold, dilute potassium permanganate loses its purple color and forms a brown solid when it is shaken with these compounds, which it turns into diols. Osmium tetroxide adds two –OH groups to these compounds the same way.
tossups.r: Bromine water also detects them by losing its orange color. For 10 points, name these unsaturated hydrocarbons whose names end in “-ene.”

tossups.p: Zaitsev’s [“ZYE-tsefs”] rule predicts that when a strong base removes HBr from an alkyl bromide, the main product is the more substituted of these compounds. Reactions like that one, which remove a small molecule from two neighboring carbon atoms, are called eliminations.
tossups.r: Removing water from alcohols also makes them. For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons with at least one carbon–carbon double bond, such as propene.

tossups.p: Georg Wittig [“VIT-ik”] shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for a reaction that uses phosphorus ylides [“ILL-idz”] to turn aldehydes and ketones into these compounds. In that reaction, the oxygen atom from the aldehyde or ketone ends up bonded to phosphorus instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons with a carbon–carbon double bond, which are unsaturated and have names ending in “-ene.”

tossups.p: Karl Ziegler and Giulio Natta [“JOO-lee-oh NAH-tah”] shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for catalysts, made from titanium compounds and aluminum alkyls, that link molecules of these compounds into long, orderly chains. Natta used such catalysts to control which way the side groups of a chain point.
tossups.r: Those catalysts make plastics such as polyethylene and polypropylene. For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons, such as ethylene, that have a carbon–carbon double bond.

tossups.p: In 1933, Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson at the British company ICI accidentally made a waxy white solid while heating the simplest of these compounds with benzaldehyde at very high pressure. That solid became the world’s most common plastic.
tossups.r: That plastic is polyethylene. For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons, including ethene, that have at least one carbon–carbon double bond.

tossups.p: Dutch chemists in the 1790s called the simplest member of this class “olefiant gas,” meaning “oil-forming gas,” because it reacts with chlorine to form an oily liquid. Factories make more of that compound than of any other organic chemical, mostly by steam cracking.
tossups.r: In plants, that compound is a gas hormone that ripens fruit. For 10 points, name this class of hydrocarbons, including ethene, that have a carbon–carbon double bond.

tossups.p: Chemists label some isomers of these compounds Z, from the German word zusammen [“tsoo-ZAH-men”], meaning “together,” and others E, from entgegen [“ent-GAY-gen”], meaning “opposite,” by using priority rules named for Cahn, Ingold, and Prelog. The Z form has its two higher-priority groups on the same side.
tossups.r: Because their key bond cannot rotate, 2-butene comes in cis and trans forms. For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons with a carbon–carbon double bond.

tossups.p: Vision begins when light flips one bond in the molecule retinal [“RET-ih-nal”] from a bent cis shape to a straight trans shape inside the protein rhodopsin [“roh-DOP-sin”]. Retinal is a long chain with several of the bonds that define this class of compounds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons, such as ethene and propene, that contain a carbon–carbon double bond.

tossups.p: In the Diels–Alder [“DEELZ AHL-der”] reaction, a diene joins with one of these compounds, called the dienophile [“dye-EE-nuh-file”], to build a six-membered ring. Otto Diels and Kurt Alder shared the 1950 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for that reaction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unsaturated hydrocarbons, such as ethylene, whose names end in “-ene” and which turn bromine water colorless.

tossups.p: Paul Sabatier [“sah-bah-TYAY”] won a Nobel Prize for using finely powdered nickel to help hydrogen add to these compounds, turning them into alkanes. Partly hydrogenating vegetable oils this way makes solid margarine but can also create trans fats, which many countries have restricted.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these unsaturated hydrocarbons, such as ethene, whose names end in “-ene.”

tossups.p: Each carbon atom in the key bond of these compounds is sp2 hybridized and trigonal planar, with bond angles near 120 degrees, because that bond is made of one sigma bond and one pi bond. Non-ring members with just one such bond have the general formula CnH2n.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hydrocarbons with at least one carbon–carbon double bond, such as ethene.

Removing water from alcohols with hot concentrated sulfuric acid makes them

E/Z names: Z from zusammen (“together”) and E from entgegen (“opposite”), using Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priorities
Vision starts when light flips a double bond in retinal from cis to trans inside rhodopsin
In the Diels–Alder reaction (1950 Nobel), one acts as the dienophile that joins a diene to make a six-membered ring

trap.title: Watch the vowel
trap.body: Alkanes (only single bonds), alkenes (a carbon–carbon double bond), and alkynes (a triple bond) differ by a single vowel, so a slip of the tongue gives a wrong answer. Players also blurt “ethylene,” the simplest example, when the question wants the whole class, or “alcohols,” since many clues describe reactions that turn these compounds into alcohols.
trap.fix: Match the vowel to the bond: a = single (saturated, “-ane”), e = double (“-ene”), y = triple (“-yne”). Bromine water turning colorless, Markovnikov’s rule, cis–trans isomers, and polyethylene all mean double bonds.
trap.line: Real answer line: Alkenes (accept alkene or olefins; prompt on unsaturated hydrocarbons; do not accept “alkanes” or “alkynes”)

topics.name: Acetic acid
topics.kicker: The sour acid in vinegar · A two-carbon carboxylic acid
topics.dates: First made from non-living materials by Hermann Kolbe, 1845
topics.briefing: Acetic acid is the compound that makes vinegar sour and sharp-smelling; household vinegar is mostly water with about 5 percent acetic acid. Bacteria make it when they turn the ethanol in apple cider or wine into vinegar. Pure acetic acid freezes into icy-looking crystals at about 17 °C, so chemists call it “glacial,” and factories make millions of tons of it every year for glue, paint, and plastics.
topics.answerHtml: Acetic acid (or ethanoic acid; accept CH3COOH; prompt on vinegar; do not accept “acid” alone or “acetone”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Monsanto process, introduced around 1970, made this compound by joining methanol with carbon monoxide over a rhodium catalyst, and BP’s newer Cativa process does the same job with iridium. Both processes need an iodide promoter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this carboxylic acid, the active ingredient in vinegar, which gives it a sour taste and sharp smell.

tossups.p: In 1845, Hermann Kolbe [“KOHL-buh”] made this compound from carbon disulfide in several steps, using only starting materials that did not come from living things. Along with Friedrich Wöhler’s [“VUR-lerz”] urea synthesis, that work helped disprove vitalism.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this two-carbon carboxylic acid, the sour compound that makes up about 5 percent of vinegar.

tossups.p: In the vapor and in nonpolar solvents, molecules of this compound pair up into ring-shaped dimers held together by two hydrogen bonds, so measuring the density of its vapor gives a molar mass nearly double its true value of 60.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this carboxylic acid, whose dilute solution in water is vinegar.

tossups.p: Pure, water-free samples of this compound freeze into icy-looking crystals at about 17 °C, a little below room temperature, so chemists call them “glacial.” Even a small amount of water lowers that freezing point, and the liquid mixes with water in any amount.
tossups.r: Vinegar is mostly water with a small amount of this compound mixed in. For 10 points, name this weak acid.

tossups.p: This compound has a pKa of about 4.76, so mixing it with its sodium salt makes a classic buffer that holds a solution near that pH. It ionizes only slightly in water, so its solution barely lights a conductivity tester’s bulb.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this two-carbon carboxylic acid, the active ingredient in vinegar, which gives it a sharp smell.

tossups.p: Reusable hand warmers hold a supersaturated solution of this compound’s sodium salt, which suddenly crystallizes and gives off heat when a small metal disc inside is clicked. That salt is also used to make “hot ice,” which hardens into a tower of crystals as it is poured onto a seed crystal.
tossups.r: That salt is called sodium acetate. For 10 points, name this weak acid, the active ingredient in vinegar.

tossups.p: Bacteria of the genus Acetobacter [“uh-SEE-toh-bak-ter”] make this compound by oxidizing ethanol, and they can form a slimy, jelly-like mat called a “mother” on top of the liquid. Making this compound this way is an aerobic process, so the bacteria need oxygen.
tossups.r: Apple cider is turned into a sour liquid this way. For 10 points, name this acid, the active ingredient in vinegar.

tossups.p: Movie studios replaced flammable nitrate film with “safety film” made from cellulose and this compound. Much of this compound also goes into polyvinyl products such as the white glue used in schools, and its anhydride turns salicylic acid into aspirin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this carboxylic acid with two carbon atoms, the sour ingredient in vinegar.

tossups.p: In cells, coenzyme A carries the two-carbon group of this acid into the Krebs cycle, where it joins a four-carbon molecule to form citrate. That two-carbon group, called acetyl, also appears in aspirin and in the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weak acid that makes vinegar sour and gives it a sharp smell.

tossups.p: Medieval and Renaissance painters used the green pigment verdigris [“VUR-dih-grees”], which was made by letting fumes of this compound attack copper plates. This compound’s lead salt, called “sugar of lead” because it tastes sweet, is poisonous.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this two-carbon carboxylic acid, which gives vinegar its sour taste and sharp smell.

tossups.p: Photographers dip film into a dilute solution of this compound, called a “stop bath,” to halt developing. Before modern factories, much of this compound came from pyroligneous [“pye-roh-LIG-nee-us”] acid, a dark liquid given off when wood is heated without air, which also yielded methanol.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this two-carbon acid that is the active ingredient in vinegar and gives it a sour taste.

tossups.p: Soaking an egg in this compound’s dilute solution for a day or two dissolves the calcium carbonate shell, leaving a rubbery “naked egg” held together by its membrane. The bubbles that form on the shell are carbon dioxide.
tossups.r: Mixing baking soda with the same solution makes a fizzy “volcano.” For 10 points, name this acid, the active ingredient in vinegar.

tossups.p: Students often find the concentration of this compound in a store-bought sample by titrating it with sodium hydroxide until the phenolphthalein indicator turns the mixture faint pink. At the endpoint, this compound has been converted into its sodium salt and water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this acid, about 5 percent of a typical bottle of vinegar.

tossups.p: Heating this compound with isoamyl alcohol and a little sulfuric acid makes “banana oil,” an ester that smells like bananas. Reacting it with ethanol makes a different ester used as a solvent in glues and some nail polish removers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this carboxylic acid whose salts are called acetates and whose dilute solution is vinegar.

tossups.p: This compound’s common name comes from acetum, the Latin word for its best-known source, and it is the second-simplest carboxylic acid after formic acid. Its molecule has a methyl group attached to a –COOH group.
tossups.r: Its conjugate base is the acetate ion. For 10 points, name this weak acid, the sour active ingredient in household vinegar.

trap.title: Not just vinegar or acid
trap.body: Vinegar is a mixture, mostly water, that contains this compound, so answering “vinegar” earns only a prompt, and answering “acid” alone is wrong because the question wants one specific compound. Players also confuse it with acetone, the sharp-smelling solvent in many nail polish removers, and with other acids from foods, such as lactic, citric, and formic acid.
trap.fix: Say the full name, “acetic acid” (or “ethanoic acid”). Formic acid has one carbon and comes from ants; citric acid is in lemons; lactic acid is in sour milk and tired muscles; acetone is a ketone with no –COOH group.
trap.line: Real answer line: Acetic acid (or ethanoic acid; accept CH3COOH; prompt on vinegar; do not accept “acid” alone or “acetone”)

topics.name: Sodium
topics.kicker: Element 11 · The soft, reactive metal in table salt
topics.briefing: Sodium is a silvery metal so soft you can cut it with a butter knife, and it reacts so violently with water that a small piece zips across the surface, fizzing out hydrogen. Humphry Davy first isolated it in 1807 by running electricity through melted caustic soda. You eat it every day in table salt, sodium chloride, and its bright yellow-orange glow has lit many streetlights.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley used the giant nerve fiber of a squid to show that ions of this element rush into a neuron at the start of each nerve impulse. A protein pump pushes three ions of this element out of a cell for every two potassium ions it brings in.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 11, which combines with chlorine to make table salt.

tossups.p: Joseph von Fraunhofer [“FROWN-hoh-fer”] labeled a pair of dark lines in the Sun’s spectrum with the letter D, and in 1859 Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen showed that vapor of this element causes them. This element’s D lines are near 589 nanometers.
tossups.r: This element gives a bright yellow-orange color in a flame test. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 11.

tossups.p: Large telescopes shine powerful lasers at a layer of this element’s atoms about 90 kilometers up, making them glow as artificial “guide stars” that help cancel the blur caused by Earth’s atmosphere. Those atoms come from meteors that burn up high in the sky.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 11, which is part of table salt.

tossups.p: Ancient Egyptians used natron, a mineral mixture rich in this element’s carbonate and bicarbonate, to dry out bodies before wrapping them as mummies, and ancient glassmakers used it as a flux. Natron also gave this element its chemical symbol.
tossups.r: That symbol comes from the Latin natrium. For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 11.

tossups.p: In a Downs cell, factories make this element by electrolysis of a molten mixture to which calcium chloride is added to lower the melting point. The liquid metal floats to the top of the cell, where it is collected without touching air.
tossups.r: Chlorine gas is made at the same time. For 10 points, name this alkali metal, which combines with chlorine to make table salt.

tossups.p: In 1807, just days after isolating potassium, Humphry Davy isolated this element by passing electric current through its molten hydroxide, which is commonly called caustic soda or lye. He used a huge battery at the Royal Institution in London.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this alkali metal, element 11, whose English name comes from “soda.”

tossups.p: This element melts at about 98 °C, so its liquid form has been used to carry heat away from the cores of fast breeder nuclear reactors. It is soft enough to cut with a butter knife, and freshly cut surfaces quickly tarnish in air.
tossups.r: It is stored under oil to keep water away. For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 11.

tossups.p: This element dissolves in liquid ammonia to make a deep blue solution full of loose electrons. When a small piece of it is dropped into water, it floats, melts into a shiny ball, and skates around as it fizzes out hydrogen gas.
tossups.r: That reaction also makes a strong base. For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 11.

tossups.p: Tetrodotoxin [“teh-TROH-doh-tok-sin”], a poison found in pufferfish, works by blocking the channels that let ions of this element into nerve cells, so nerve signals cannot fire. Doctors call too little of this element in the blood hyponatremia [“hy-poh-nuh-TREE-mee-uh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 11, which joins chlorine in table salt.

tossups.p: Many car airbags were once inflated by heating this element’s azide, which breaks down in a split second to release nitrogen gas. Low-pressure streetlights filled with this element’s vapor give off a single, almost pure color of light that astronomers can easily filter out.
tossups.r: Those lamps glow yellow-orange. For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 11, found in table salt.

tossups.p: Nicolas Leblanc’s [“luh-BLAHN’s”] process, patented in 1791, made soda ash, a carbonate of this element, using sulfuric acid, coal, and limestone among its ingredients, until Ernest Solvay’s cleaner process, which recycles ammonia, replaced it. Soda ash is a key ingredient in ordinary window glass, called soda-lime glass.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this alkali metal, element 11, that sits just above potassium in group 1.

tossups.p: Glassblowers wear goggles made with didymium [“dye-DIM-ee-um”] glass to block the intense glare this element gives off in hot glass. A tiny trace of this element can hide other flame-test colors, so chemists look through blue cobalt glass when testing for potassium.
tossups.r: This element gives a bright yellow-orange flame. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 11.

tossups.p: In 1908, Kikunae Ikeda [“kee-koo-NAH-eh ee-KEH-dah”] identified glutamate as the source of the savory taste he called umami and patented a way to make a compound of glutamic acid and this element. He had found glutamate in kombu, a seaweed used in Japanese soup stock. That flavor enhancer is abbreviated MSG.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 11, whose chloride is ordinary table salt.

tossups.p: The Hubble Space Telescope detected this element in the atmosphere of the planet HD 209458 b, the first atmosphere found on a planet outside the solar system. Sunlight also pushes atoms of this element out of Mercury’s thin atmosphere into a long, comet-like tail.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 11, which gives a yellow-orange flame test.

tossups.p: This element’s electron configuration is written [Ne] 3s¹, because its atoms have a single electron in the third shell. Removing that electron takes little energy, but removing a second one would take about nine times as much, so this element forms only +1 ions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 11, which sits between lithium and potassium in group 1.

trap.title: Element, not table salt
trap.body: Many clues for this element are really about its compounds, like table salt, baking soda, lye, and soda ash, so players blurt “salt” or “sodium chloride,” which are wrong when the question asks for the element. Potassium, just below it in group 1, is the other trap: both are soft, both react with water, Humphry Davy isolated both in 1807, and the same pump moves both across cell membranes.
trap.fix: Answer with the element whenever the question says “this element,” even if the clue names one of its compounds. A yellow-orange flame, element 11, natron, the D lines, and streetlights point here; a lilac flame, element 19, potash, and bananas point to potassium.

topics.name: Robert Bunsen
topics.kicker: German chemist · Spectroscopy pioneer who found cesium and rubidium
topics.briefing: Robert Bunsen was a German chemist whose name is on the gas burner in almost every school lab, though his university’s mechanic, Peter Desaga, actually built it in 1855. With physicist Gustav Kirchhoff, Bunsen showed that every element glows with its own pattern of colored lines, and the pair used that method to discover two new elements, cesium and rubidium. Earlier, an exploding arsenic compound had cost him the sight of one eye.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This chemist lost the sight of one eye when a cacodyl [“KAK-oh-dil”] compound exploded in his laboratory. Cacodyl compounds contain arsenic and get their name from the Greek word for “stinking,” and studying them gave this chemist a dangerous case of arsenic poisoning.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist who, with Gustav Kirchhoff, discovered cesium and rubidium and has a common lab burner named for him.

tossups.p: In 1841, this scientist invented a cheaper battery cell by replacing the expensive platinum electrode of William Grove’s cell with carbon. He later used banks of those cells to make magnesium by electrolysis, and with Augustus Matthiessen he made lithium metal in larger amounts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist whose name is on a gas burner found in school science labs.

tossups.p: Working with his student Henry Roscoe, this chemist showed that the amount of chemical change light causes depends on its brightness multiplied by how long it shines, a rule called the reciprocity law. They measured light by how fast it made hydrogen and chlorine combine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist who taught for decades at Heidelberg and names a lab burner.

tossups.p: In 1846, this scientist traveled to Iceland, where he measured temperatures deep inside the Great Geysir [“GAY-seer”] and explained that a geyser erupts when water deep in its tube, heated above 100 °C under pressure, suddenly flashes into steam.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist who discovered cesium and rubidium with Gustav Kirchhoff.

tossups.p: In 1870, this chemist invented an ice calorimeter that measures small amounts of heat by tracking how much the volume of an ice-and-water mixture shrinks as the ice melts. He used it to measure the specific heats of rare metals available only in tiny samples.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist who, with Gustav Kirchhoff, founded the use of spectroscopy to identify elements.

tossups.p: In 1860, this chemist and a physicist partner boiled down huge amounts of mineral water from Dürkheim and found a new element by its two bright blue spectral lines. They named it from the Latin for “sky blue.”
tossups.r: That element is cesium. For 10 points, name this German chemist who worked with Gustav Kirchhoff and names a lab burner.

tossups.p: In 1861, this chemist and his partner found a new element in the mineral lepidolite [“lep-ID-uh-lite”] by spotting two dark red lines in its spectrum, so they named it from the Latin for “deep red.” It was the second element they discovered together.
tossups.r: That element is rubidium. For 10 points, name this German chemist who worked with Gustav Kirchhoff.

tossups.p: This chemist and a physicist partner showed in 1859 that the dark Fraunhofer [“FROWN-hoh-fer”] lines in sunlight match the bright lines given off by heated elements, revealing, for example, that the Sun contains sodium. That work made it possible to learn what stars are made of.
tossups.r: His partner was Gustav Kirchhoff. For 10 points, name this German chemist who has a lab burner named for him.

tossups.p: This chemist taught at the University of Heidelberg from 1852 until he retired in 1889, and one of his students there, Lothar Meyer, later drew up an early version of the periodic table. Before Heidelberg, he taught at Marburg and Breslau.
tossups.r: The university mechanic Peter Desaga [“deh-ZAH-gah”] built the gas burner named for him. For 10 points, name this German chemist.

tossups.p: In 1877, this chemist and his longtime partner became the first two winners of the Royal Society’s Davy Medal, honoring their work in spectrum analysis. That partner is also known for laws of electric circuits.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist who discovered cesium and rubidium and names a common lab burner.

tossups.p: This chemist analyzed the gases escaping from iron blast furnaces in Germany and, with Lyon Playfair, in England, showing that much of the heat from the fuel was being wasted. He also invented a grease-spot photometer for comparing the brightness of two lights.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist, the namesake of a common lab gas burner.

tossups.p: In 1859, this chemist and a physicist partner built one of the first spectroscopes for chemical analysis, using a prism to spread the light from a flame into bright lines. They showed that each element always gives off the same lines, no matter which compound it is in.
tossups.r: That partner was Gustav Kirchhoff. For 10 points, name this German chemist, the namesake of a gas burner used in school labs.

tossups.p: The method of spectrum analysis that this chemist helped develop quickly led others to new elements: William Crookes found thallium by its green line in 1861, and Ferdinand Reich and Theodor Richter found indium by its indigo line in 1863.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist who used that method with Gustav Kirchhoff to discover cesium and rubidium.

tossups.p: In 1834, this chemist and the doctor Arnold Berthold showed that freshly made hydrated iron oxide works as an antidote for arsenic poisoning, because it binds the arsenic into a compound that does not dissolve.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist who discovered cesium and rubidium with Gustav Kirchhoff and names a lab burner.

tossups.p: Germany’s main society for physical chemistry is named for this chemist, who was born in Göttingen [“GUR-ting-en”] in 1811 and earned his doctorate at the university there, where his father was a professor. He died in Heidelberg in 1899.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chemist who discovered cesium and rubidium with Gustav Kirchhoff and has a lab burner named for him.

trap.title: The man, not his burner
trap.body: Robert Bunsen and the physicist Gustav Kirchhoff worked as a team, so spectroscopy clues, the Sun’s dark lines, and the discovery of cesium and rubidium fit both men. Kirchhoff also has his own laws of electric circuits and of radiation, which are not Bunsen’s. And answering “Bunsen burner” when a question asks for a person is wrong.
trap.fix: Chemistry-lab clues, like arsenic compounds, batteries, the ice calorimeter, geysers, and the burner, mean Bunsen; circuit laws and laws of radiation mean Kirchhoff. If a question asks for “this man” or “this chemist,” give just the person’s name.

topics.name: Polymers
topics.kicker: Giant molecules built from repeating units · Plastics, nylon, and DNA
topics.dates: Chain idea proposed by Hermann Staudinger, 1920
topics.briefing: A polymer is a giant molecule made of thousands of small units, called monomers, linked like beads on a necklace. Nature builds polymers such as starch, silk, rubber, and DNA, while chemists build plastics like polyethylene. In 1935 Wallace Carothers of DuPont invented nylon, which soon replaced silk in stockings, and in 1965 Stephanie Kwolek invented Kevlar, a fiber used in bulletproof vests.
topics.answerHtml: Polymers (accept polymerization; prompt on plastics or macromolecules; do not accept “monomers”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Hermann Staudinger [“SHTOW-ding-er”] won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for arguing that these substances are enormous molecules held together by ordinary covalent bonds, not loose clumps of small molecules. Many chemists rejected his idea when he proposed it in 1920.
tossups.r: Nylon and Kevlar are synthetic examples. For 10 points, name these giant molecules built from many small repeating units called monomers.

tossups.p: Jöns Jacob Berzelius [“ber-ZEE-lee-us”] coined the name for these substances in 1833, though he meant something different from its modern meaning. John Wesley Hyatt made celluloid from one of them, partly as a substitute for the ivory in billiard balls.
tossups.r: Their name comes from Greek words meaning “many parts.” For 10 points, name these giant chain molecules that make up plastics.

tossups.p: One of these substances, nylon 6,6, is named for the six carbon atoms in each of its two starting materials, one of which is adipic acid. Wallace Carothers led the DuPont team that first made nylon in 1935, and it soon replaced silk in women’s stockings.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these giant molecules, which also include Teflon and polyethylene, made of many repeating units.

tossups.p: In Kevlar, hydrogen bonds join neighboring chains of this kind of molecule into strong, flat sheets. Stephanie Kwolek [“KWOH-lek”] invented that fiber at DuPont in 1965, and it is used in bulletproof vests.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these giant molecules, such as nylon and polyethylene, that are made of many repeating units called monomers.

tossups.p: Leo Baekeland [“BAY-kuh-land”] made his first fortune selling his Velox photographic paper to George Eastman, then in 1907 invented Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, from phenol and formaldehyde. Bakelite is a thermoset, so once it hardens it cannot be melted and reshaped.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these giant molecules made of repeating units, the main ingredients of all plastics.

tossups.p: Charles Goodyear discovered in 1839 that heating natural rubber with sulfur made it tough instead of sticky, because sulfur atoms form cross-links between these long molecules. Natural rubber is one of these substances, built from units of isoprene [“EYE-soh-preen”].
tossups.r: PVC and polystyrene are synthetic examples. For 10 points, name these giant chain molecules made of monomers.

tossups.p: Roy Plunkett discovered Teflon in 1938 when a cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene [“tet-ruh-floor-oh-ETH-uh-leen”] gas seemed empty but held a slippery white powder. Teflon, polyethylene, and PVC are all addition types of these substances, which form when small molecules with double bonds link up without giving off anything.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these huge molecules made by linking many small units called monomers into chains.

tossups.p: Both nylon and the proteins in your body are polyamides, a class of these substances whose units are joined by amide bonds. Those bonds form in condensation reactions, which give off a small molecule such as water each time two units link.
tossups.r: Polyester is another example. For 10 points, name these giant molecules made of many repeating units called monomers.

tossups.p: Karl Ziegler and Giulio Natta [“JOO-lee-oh NAH-tah”] shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for catalysts, made from titanium and aluminum compounds, that link small molecules into long, orderly chains. Those catalysts made it practical to produce two of these substances: polypropylene and the high-density polyethylene used in milk jugs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these huge molecules, which include all plastics, made of repeating units called monomers.

tossups.p: In 1933, Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson at the British company ICI accidentally made a waxy white solid while heating ethylene at very high pressure. That solid, polyethylene, became the world’s most common plastic and a classic example of these substances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these giant chain molecules, which also include nylon, starch, and DNA.

tossups.p: In 1941, John Rex Whinfield and James Dickson patented one of these substances, PET, which is used for soda bottles and Dacron fabric. Plastics are sorted by recycling codes from 1 to 7, and PET is code 1.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these giant molecules, such as nylon and polyethylene, made of many repeating units.

tossups.p: In the “nylon rope trick,” a continuous strand is pulled from the boundary between two liquids that don’t mix, as new material keeps forming where they meet. Silk and wool are natural materials made of these substances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these long-chain molecules, such as nylon, made from repeating units called monomers.

tossups.p: Below a temperature called the glass transition, many of these materials are hard and brittle, but above it they turn soft and rubbery. Thermoplastic types can be melted and reshaped again and again, while thermosets, like Bakelite, stay hard once they set.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these giant molecules built from repeating units, which make up plastics.

tossups.p: Chitin [“KY-tin”], which makes up the hard outer skeletons of insects and crabs, is one of these substances. Cellulose and starch are both chains of glucose, but their glucose units are linked in slightly different ways, so people can digest starch but not cellulose.
tossups.r: Proteins and DNA are other natural examples. For 10 points, name these giant molecules built from small units called monomers.

tossups.p: Neoprene, a synthetic rubber used in wetsuits, came out of Wallace Carothers’s research group at DuPont in 1930, five years before that group first made nylon. Both neoprene and nylon are synthetic examples of these substances.
tossups.r: Polystyrene is another. For 10 points, name these giant molecules made of repeating units called monomers.

trap.title: The chain, not one link
trap.body: Polymer tossups are full of single examples, like nylon, Kevlar, Teflon, and polyethylene, and of the small units they are built from, so players blurt one example or say “monomers.” Others hear about DNA and mix up the molecules with polymerase, the enzyme that builds DNA chains. Saying “plastics” earns only a prompt, because plastics are just one kind of polymer.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these substances” or “these giant molecules” and the clues jump between nylon, rubber, starch, and plastics, give the class name. Say “monomers” only for the small repeating units themselves, and name one example only for “this plastic” or “this fiber.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Polymers (accept polymerization; prompt on plastics or macromolecules; do not accept “monomers”)

topics.name: Phosphorus
topics.kicker: Element 15 · The glowing element in matches, bones, and DNA
topics.briefing: In 1669, the German alchemist Hennig Brand boiled down huge amounts of urine, hoping to find the secret of making gold, and instead got a waxy substance that glowed in the dark. He had found phosphorus, whose name means “light-bearer” in Greek. Its red form coats the striking strip on a matchbox, and phosphate groups containing it hold together your DNA and help ATP power your cells.
topics.answerHtml: Phosphorus (accept P; accept white phosphorus or red phosphorus; do not accept “phosphate”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Joseph Wright of Derby painted an alchemist kneeling beside a glowing flask as he discovers this element. In real life, Hennig Brand first made it in 1669 by boiling down large amounts of urine while searching for the philosopher’s stone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15, whose red form is used on the strips for striking matches.

tossups.p: Despite this element’s name, the faint green glow of its white form is not phosphorescence but chemiluminescence, caused by a slow reaction with oxygen in the air. That white form can burst into flame on its own, so it is stored under water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15, found in the phosphate groups of DNA.

tossups.p: The 1906 Berne Convention banned this element’s white form from matches, because factory workers who handled it could develop a bone disease of the jaw nicknamed “phossy jaw.” Strike-anywhere match heads later used a safer compound of this element and sulfur instead.
tossups.r: Safety matches use its red form on the striking strip. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: In 1952, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase labeled viral DNA with a radioactive isotope of this element and viral protein with radioactive sulfur, helping show that DNA is the genetic material. Hennig Brand had first isolated this element from urine in 1669.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element found in the phosphate groups of DNA and ATP, number 15 on the periodic table.

tossups.p: Antoine Lavoisier [“lah-vwah-zee-AY”] showed that this element and sulfur gain mass when they burn, because they combine with part of the air, helping overthrow the phlogiston theory. Burning this element makes a white smoke of its oxide, which soaks up water so strongly that chemists use it as a drying agent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15, whose red form is used on the striking strips of matchboxes.

tossups.p: This element shares its name with the ancient Greek name for the planet Venus seen as the morning star, since both names mean “light-bearer.” This element’s white form glows faintly in the dark as it slowly reacts with oxygen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, number 15 on the periodic table, used in matches and fertilizers.

tossups.p: In 1842, John Bennet Lawes patented a fertilizer called superphosphate, made by treating rock rich in this element with sulfuric acid. Seabird droppings called guano, dug from islands off Peru, were another important early source of this plant nutrient.
tossups.r: Fertilizers supply it along with nitrogen and potassium. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: Unlike the carbon and nitrogen cycles, the cycle of this element has no major stage as a gas in the atmosphere, so it moves mainly through rocks, soil, water, and living things. Weathering rocks slowly release this element as ions that plants absorb through their roots.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, a key nutrient in fertilizer along with nitrogen and potassium.

tossups.p: Many U.S. states limited this element’s compounds in laundry and dishwasher detergents, because wastewater carrying them fed huge algal blooms in lakes, a process called eutrophication [“yoo-troh-fih-KAY-shun”]. Runoff from fertilized farm fields carries this element into rivers and lakes too.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15, which fertilizers supply along with nitrogen and potassium.

tossups.p: Black, the most stable form of this element, has stacked, puckered layers like graphite, and sheets one atom thick can be peeled off it much like graphene. Heating this element’s white form without air turns it into a red form that is far less dangerous to handle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, number 15, whose red form coats the strips used to strike safety matches.

tossups.p: About a century after this element was first found, Johan Gahn and Carl Wilhelm Scheele [“SHAY-luh”] learned to make it from bone ash, a far richer source than urine. Bones and teeth get their hardness from a calcium mineral called hydroxyapatite [“hy-DROK-see-AP-uh-tite”], which contains this element.
tossups.r: Phosphate groups containing it link the sugars in DNA. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: Cell membranes are built from two layers of molecules whose water-loving heads contain this element and whose tails are fatty acids. Inside cells, enzymes called kinases switch many proteins on or off by attaching groups containing this element to them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element found in ATP and in the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA.

tossups.p: Morocco holds most of the world’s known reserves of a rock that is mined for this element, and large deposits are also mined in Florida. Many plants team up with root fungi called mycorrhizae [“my-koh-RYE-zee”] to help gather this nutrient from the soil.
tossups.r: Fertilizer labels list its amount second, after nitrogen and before potassium. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: Each molecule of this element’s white form has four atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron, and the strain in their tightly bent bonds makes that form very reactive. That white form must be kept under water, because it can catch fire on its own in air.
tossups.r: Its safer red form is used on the strips for striking matches. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: An acid containing this element gives cola drinks their tangy taste and is used in rust removers that turn rust into a protective coating. Many insecticides, such as malathion [“MAL-uh-thy-on”], are organic compounds of this element.
tossups.r: Its phosphate groups are in ATP and DNA. For 10 points, name this element, whose red form is used to strike matches.

Its red form coats the striking strip on safety-match boxes
Found in the phosphate groups of DNA, RNA, and ATP
One of the three main nutrients in fertilizer, with nitrogen and potassium
Hennig Brand discovered it in 1669 by boiling down urine while searching for the philosopher’s stone
Its name means “light-bearer” in Greek, because its white form glows in the dark
White form: toxic, waxy, made of four-atom tetrahedral molecules, and so reactive that it is stored under water
Heating the white form without air makes the much safer red form
Bones and teeth are hardened by hydroxyapatite, a calcium mineral containing it
Runoff of its compounds from detergents and farms feeds algal blooms in lakes (eutrophication)
The heads of phospholipids, the molecules that form cell membranes, contain it
Its cycle, unlike the carbon and nitrogen cycles, has no major gas stage in the atmosphere
The white form’s glow is chemiluminescence from a slow reaction with oxygen, not phosphorescence
Joseph Wright of Derby painted an alchemist kneeling beside a glowing flask as he discovers it
The 1906 Berne Convention banned its white form from matches because of “phossy jaw,” a bone disease of match workers
Strike-anywhere match heads contain a compound of it and sulfur; safety match heads hold potassium chlorate instead
Hershey and Chase (1952) labeled viral DNA with a radioactive isotope of it and viral protein with radioactive sulfur
Lavoisier showed that it and sulfur gain mass when burned, helping overthrow the phlogiston theory
Its oxide, the white smoke made when it burns, soaks up water so well that it is used as a drying agent
Its name was also the ancient Greek name for Venus as the morning star
Black, its most stable form, has layers like graphite that can be peeled into sheets one atom thick
About a century after its discovery, Johan Gahn and Carl Wilhelm Scheele learned to make it from bone ash instead of urine
John Bennet Lawes patented superphosphate fertilizer (1842), made from rock rich in it plus sulfuric acid; seabird guano was another source
Morocco holds most of the world’s known reserves of the rock mined for it; Florida has large deposits too
Its acid gives cola its tang and turns rust into a protective coating; insecticides like malathion contain it
Enzymes called kinases switch proteins on or off by attaching groups containing it
Root fungi called mycorrhizae help plants gather it from the soil

trap.title: Element, not phosphate
trap.body: Many clues about DNA, ATP, bones, and fertilizer mention “phosphate,” a group made of this element bonded to oxygen, so players blurt “phosphate” when the question wants the element. “Phosphor” and “phosphorescence” are traps too: despite the name, white phosphorus glows because of a slow reaction with oxygen (chemiluminescence), not phosphorescence.
trap.fix: If the question says “this element” or gives the atomic number 15, say phosphorus. Phosphate is the answer only for “this ion” or “this group.” Nitrogen, directly above it, is element 7 and makes up 78 percent of the air.
trap.line: Real answer line: Phosphorus (accept P; accept white phosphorus or red phosphorus; do not accept “phosphate”)

topics.name: Methane
topics.kicker: CH₄, the simplest hydrocarbon · The main ingredient of natural gas
topics.briefing: Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon: one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms. It is the main ingredient of the natural gas that heats homes and fuels stoves, and it bubbles up from swamps, which is why it was once called “marsh gas.” Cows burp it out as microbes in their stomachs digest grass, and on Saturn’s moon Titan it falls as rain and fills lakes.
topics.answerHtml: Methane (accept CH4 or marsh gas; prompt on natural gas; do not accept “ethane” or “methanol”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1776, Alessandro Volta collected bubbles of this gas by stirring the mud along the shores of Lake Maggiore [“mah-JOR-ay”], and he showed that it could burn. Coal miners feared pockets of this gas, which they called “firedamp,” because it could explode underground.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas, the simplest hydrocarbon and the main ingredient in natural gas.

tossups.p: Humphry Davy’s 1815 safety lamp surrounded its flame with fine wire gauze so that the flame could not ignite this gas, which often caused explosions in coal mines. With plenty of air, this gas burns with a hot blue flame in laboratory Bunsen burners.
tossups.r: Cows burp it out as they digest grass. For 10 points, name this gas made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms.

tossups.p: In 1944, Gerard Kuiper [“KY-per”] detected this gas in the atmosphere of a moon, the first evidence that any moon has an atmosphere. Sunlight breaks this gas apart high in that moon’s air, and the pieces join into an orange haze of particles called tholins [“THOH-linz”].
tossups.r: That moon, Titan, has lakes of liquid ethane and this compound. For 10 points, name this simplest hydrocarbon.

tossups.p: On the seafloor and in permafrost, molecules of this gas are trapped inside cages of frozen water, forming a substance nicknamed “fire ice” because a lump of it can burn. Thawing permafrost can also release this gas as microbes break down ancient plant remains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this greenhouse gas, the main component of the natural gas used for heating homes.

tossups.p: In steam reforming, this compound reacts with steam over a nickel catalyst to make most of the hydrogen used in the Haber process. Burning one mole of this compound releases about 890 kilojoules of heat and makes carbon dioxide and water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas, the main ingredient of the natural gas burned in stoves and furnaces.

tossups.p: In ultraviolet light, chlorine atoms can replace this compound’s hydrogen atoms one at a time, eventually producing chloroform and then carbon tetrachloride. Its molecule is a perfect tetrahedron, with bond angles of about 109.5 degrees.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this simplest alkane, a gas with one carbon atom that makes up most of natural gas.

tossups.p: In a famous experiment in the 1950s, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey [“YOOR-ee”] sent electric sparks through a flask of water vapor, hydrogen, ammonia, and this gas, producing several amino acids. Archaea [“ar-KEE-uh”] that live without oxygen make this gas as a waste product.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this simplest hydrocarbon, the main ingredient in the natural gas burned in kitchen stoves.

tossups.p: This gas absorbs red light, which helps give Uranus and Neptune their blue colors. Water, ammonia, and this compound make up much of the hot, slushy “ices” deep inside those two planets, which are called ice giants.
tossups.r: On Earth, it is the main ingredient of natural gas. For 10 points, name this simplest hydrocarbon.

tossups.p: Microbes living in the rumen [“ROO-men”], the first stomach chamber of cattle, sheep, and goats, produce this gas as they help break down grass, a process called enteric fermentation. Scientists have tested adding certain seaweeds to cattle feed to cut down on this gas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this greenhouse gas that cows burp out, the main ingredient of natural gas.

tossups.p: Because this gas has no smell of its own, gas companies add sulfur compounds called thiols, or mercaptans [“mer-CAP-tanz”], so that people can notice leaks. This gas is lighter than air, so it rises when it escapes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this main ingredient of the natural gas piped into homes, the simplest hydrocarbon.

tossups.p: Linus Pauling explained the shape of this molecule by mixing one s orbital and three p orbitals on its central atom into four sp³ hybrid orbitals. Those orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles of about 109.5 degrees.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms, the main part of natural gas.

tossups.p: Wetlands are the largest natural source of this gas, and rice paddies, landfills, and termites also give it off as microbes break down plant matter and garbage without oxygen. The amount of this gas in Earth’s air has more than doubled since the Industrial Revolution began.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this greenhouse gas, the main ingredient of natural gas, which cows burp out.

tossups.p: Cooled to about minus 162 degrees Celsius, this compound turns into a liquid, so special tanker ships can carry it across oceans. Its tiny molecules attract one another so weakly that it is a gas at room temperature, unlike larger hydrocarbons such as octane.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this simplest alkane, the main component of the natural gas used to heat many homes.

tossups.p: NASA’s Curiosity rover has measured changing amounts of this gas in the air of Mars’s Gale Crater, which interests scientists because living things on Earth make much of it. On Earth, this gas also forms underground as heat and pressure act on the buried remains of ancient organisms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas, the simplest hydrocarbon, which makes up most of the natural gas burned in stoves.

tossups.p: This gas lasts only about a decade in the air before it breaks down, mostly by reacting with hydroxyl radicals, while carbon dioxide lingers for centuries. Leaks from wells, pipelines, and coal mines release large amounts of this gas.
tossups.r: Ton for ton, this greenhouse gas traps far more heat than carbon dioxide. For 10 points, name this simplest hydrocarbon.

trap.title: Not natural gas or methanol
trap.body: Natural gas is a mixture that is mostly methane, so “natural gas” earns only a prompt. Methane also has close cousins with similar names: ethane (two carbons), propane (three carbons, the fuel in many grills), and methanol (an alcohol with an –OH group, also called wood alcohol). Naming one of those loses the tossup.
trap.fix: “Simplest hydrocarbon,” “one carbon and four hydrogens,” cows, Titan, firedamp, and Volta all mean methane, so say methane instead of natural gas. Two carbons mean ethane, grill tanks mean propane, and an –OH group means methanol.
trap.line: Real answer line: Methane (accept CH4 or marsh gas; prompt on natural gas; do not accept “ethane” or “methanol”)

topics.name: Catalysts
topics.kicker: Speed up reactions without being used up · From enzymes to car exhaust
topics.briefing: A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up, so a tiny amount can work again and again. It gives the reaction an easier path with a lower activation energy, like a tunnel through a mountain instead of a climb over it. Your body runs on biological catalysts called enzymes, iron catalysts help make much of the world’s fertilizer, and the platinum, palladium, and rhodium in a car’s catalytic converter clean up its exhaust.
topics.answerHtml: Catalysts (or catalysis; accept word forms like catalyze; do not accept “enzymes,” “inhibitors,” or “activation energy”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Jöns Jacob Berzelius [“ber-ZEE-lee-us”] coined the name for the action of these substances in 1835, from a Greek word meaning “loosening” or “dissolving.” In the contact process for making sulfuric acid, vanadium(V) oxide acts as one of these substances, helping sulfur dioxide combine with oxygen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances that speed up a chemical reaction without being used up.

tossups.p: Wilhelm Ostwald [“OST-vahlt”] won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on reaction rates, equilibrium, and these substances. His namesake process for making nitric acid passes ammonia and air over one of them, a gauze made of platinum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as enzymes in living things, that speed up reactions without being consumed.

tossups.p: In 1823, Johann Döbereiner [“DUR-buh-ry-ner”] built a lighter in which a jet of hydrogen burst into flame when it hit spongy platinum, which acted as one of these substances. These substances do not change how much product a reversible reaction makes; they only help it reach equilibrium faster.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, like the metals in a car’s exhaust system, that speed up reactions.

tossups.p: Paul Sabatier [“sah-bah-TYAY”] shared the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for showing that finely powdered nickel acts as one of these substances when hydrogen is added to carbon compounds. That reaction is used to turn liquid vegetable oils into solid margarine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances that speed up a reaction by lowering its activation energy, without being used up.

tossups.p: Karl Ziegler and Giulio Natta [“JOO-lee-oh NAH-tah”] won the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for substances of this kind, made from titanium and aluminum compounds, that link small molecules into plastics such as polypropylene. Likewise, iron helps nitrogen and hydrogen combine in the Haber process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, including enzymes, that speed up chemical reactions without being consumed.

tossups.p: Gerhard Ertl [“AIR-tul”] won the 2007 Nobel Prize for showing how reactions happen on the surfaces of solid substances of this kind, such as the iron used to make ammonia. Solid ones that work on gases are called heterogeneous, because they are in a different phase from the reactants.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances that speed up reactions but come out unchanged at the end.

tossups.p: Richard Heck, Ei-ichi Negishi [“neh-GEE-shee”], and Akira Suzuki shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for reactions that use palladium as one of these substances to join carbon atoms together. Chemists call these substances homogeneous when they are dissolved in the same phase as the reactants.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, including enzymes, that speed up reactions without being used up.

tossups.p: Benjamin List and David MacMillan won the 2021 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for showing that small carbon-based molecules, not just metals, can act as these substances. Their methods help chemists make only one mirror-image form of a molecule, which matters for many medicines.
tossups.r: Enzymes are biological examples of these substances. For 10 points, name these substances that speed up reactions without being consumed.

tossups.p: Porous aluminum silicate minerals called zeolites [“ZEE-oh-lites”] act as these substances in oil refineries, helping crack large petroleum molecules into gasoline. In a reaction mechanism, one of these substances is used up in an early step and given back in a later step.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, which speed up reactions by lowering their activation energy.

tossups.p: A single chlorine atom from CFCs can destroy as many as 100,000 ozone molecules, because it acts as one of these substances and is freed again after each cycle. Unlike a reaction intermediate, one of these substances is present both before and after a reaction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances that speed up a reaction without being used up, such as enzymes.

tossups.p: In stars more massive than the Sun, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen nuclei act as these substances in a cycle that fuses hydrogen into helium, as Hans Bethe [“BAY-tuh”] explained. That CNO cycle and the proton–proton chain are the two main ways stars fuse hydrogen.
tossups.r: On Earth, enzymes are biological examples of these substances. For 10 points, name these substances that speed up reactions without being consumed.

tossups.p: Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as one of these substances when a carboxylic acid and an alcohol combine to form an ester and water. In chemical equations, these substances are often written above the reaction arrow instead of with the reactants, because they come out of the reaction unchanged.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances that speed up chemical reactions and can be used over and over.

tossups.p: These substances do not change a reaction’s overall enthalpy change or its equilibrium constant, because they speed up the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor. As a result, they help a reversible reaction reach equilibrium sooner without changing where that equilibrium lies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy, without being used up.

tossups.p: Lead and sulfur compounds can “poison” these substances by sticking to their surfaces and blocking them. For example, carbon monoxide and sulfur compounds must be removed from the gases fed over the iron one used in the Haber process.
tossups.r: Cars with platinum and rhodium exhaust devices must burn unleaded gasoline. For 10 points, name these substances that speed up reactions without being used up.

tossups.p: In the “elephant toothpaste” demonstration, potassium iodide acts as one of these substances, making hydrogen peroxide break down so fast that a column of soapy foam shoots out of a flask. Black manganese dioxide powder plays the same role when chemists make oxygen gas from hydrogen peroxide.
tossups.r: The enzyme catalase does this job in living cells. For 10 points, name these substances that speed up reactions without being used up.
