They work by providing a different pathway with a lower activation energy
Enzymes are biological examples, usually proteins
Platinum, palladium, and rhodium in car exhaust systems turn carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide
In chemical equations they are often written above the arrow, because they come out unchanged
They speed up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so they don’t change where an equilibrium lies
They don’t change a reaction’s overall enthalpy change
Iron speeds up the Haber process, which makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen
Vanadium(V) oxide works in the contact process for sulfuric acid; platinum works in the Ostwald process for nitric acid
Heterogeneous ones are in a different phase from the reactants, like a solid metal with gases; homogeneous ones are in the same phase
Potassium iodide (in “elephant toothpaste”), manganese dioxide, and the enzyme catalase make hydrogen peroxide break down fast
In a mechanism, one is used up in an early step and given back later; an intermediate is made and then used up
Inhibitors do the opposite job, slowing reactions down
Lead and sulfur compounds can poison them by blocking their surfaces, so cars with exhaust converters need unleaded gasoline
Jöns Jacob Berzelius coined the name in 1835 from a Greek word meaning “loosening” or “dissolving”
Wilhelm Ostwald won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on them, reaction rates, and equilibrium
Johann Döbereiner’s 1823 lighter lit a jet of hydrogen with spongy platinum
Paul Sabatier (1912 Nobel) used powdered nickel to add hydrogen to carbon compounds, as in making margarine
Karl Ziegler and Giulio Natta (1963 Nobel) used titanium and aluminum compounds to make plastics like polypropylene
Gerhard Ertl won the 2007 Nobel Prize for showing how reactions happen on solid surfaces, such as iron in the Haber process
Richard Heck, Ei-ichi Negishi, and Akira Suzuki shared the 2010 Nobel Prize for palladium reactions that join carbon atoms
Benjamin List and David MacMillan won the 2021 Nobel Prize for small carbon-based molecules that do this job
Zeolites, porous aluminum silicate minerals, help crack petroleum into gasoline
Chlorine atoms from CFCs act as one, so a single atom can destroy as many as 100,000 ozone molecules
Carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen nuclei act as them in the CNO cycle that powers stars heavier than the Sun, as Hans Bethe explained
Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as one when a carboxylic acid and an alcohol combine into an ester

trap.title: The helper, not its effect
trap.body: Catalysts work by lowering activation energy, so tossups on one are full of clues about the other. Enzymes are biological catalysts, but they are a separate, more specific answer line, and inhibitors do the opposite job. The catalytic converter in a car is a device that holds catalysts, not the answer itself.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these substances” that speed up reactions and come out unchanged, say catalysts. If it asks for “this quantity” or “this energy barrier,” say activation energy. Name enzymes only when the question asks specifically for biological molecules or proteins.
trap.line: Real answer line: Catalysts (or catalysis; accept word forms like catalyze; do not accept “enzymes,” “inhibitors,” or “activation energy”)

topics.name: Aluminum
topics.kicker: Element 13 · The light, corrosion-resistant metal in cans and airplanes
topics.dates: First made in 1825; cheap after the Hall–Héroult process, 1886
topics.briefing: Aluminum is the most common metal in Earth’s crust, yet it was once so hard to purify that it cost about as much as silver, and in 1884 a small aluminum pyramid was set on top of the Washington Monument. Two years later, Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult each found a cheap way to make it using electricity. It is used in soda cans, foil, and airplanes, and recycling it saves about 95 percent of the energy needed to make new metal.
topics.answerHtml: Aluminum (or aluminium; accept Al; do not accept “alumina” or “aluminum oxide”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The American and French chemists who invented this element’s main production method were both born in 1863, both died in 1914, and made their discovery independently in 1886. Their method passes electricity through this element’s oxide dissolved in a molten mineral called cryolite.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this light metal with atomic number 13, which is used to make soda cans.

tossups.p: In 1884, a 100-ounce pyramid of this metal, which was then about as costly as silver, was set on top of the Washington Monument. Just two years later, inventors found a cheap way to make this metal using electricity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 13, whose main ore is bauxite.

tossups.p: According to a popular story, the French emperor Napoleon III served his most honored guests with cutlery made of this metal, while the other guests had to make do with gold. Napoleon III supported Henri Sainte-Claire Deville’s [“sant-CLAIR duh-VEEL”] research into making this metal more cheaply.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, number 13, that became cheap after the Hall–Héroult [“ay-ROO”] process was invented in 1886.

tossups.p: Hans Christian Ørsted [“UR-sted”] made an impure sample of this metal in 1825, and Friedrich Wöhler [“VUR-ler”] made a purer sample two years later by heating its chloride with potassium. Humphry Davy had named this element after alum, a salt used in dyeing cloth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this light metal with atomic number 13, which a thin oxide layer protects from corrosion.

tossups.p: Dmitri Mendeleev [“men-duh-LAY-ef”] predicted the properties of gallium before it was found, naming the missing element by adding the prefix “eka-” to the name of this element, which sits directly above it. This element’s oxide is amphoteric, meaning it reacts with both acids and bases.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 13, used in soda cans and kitchen foil.

tossups.p: In the Bayer process, hot sodium hydroxide dissolves this element’s oxide out of crushed ore, leaving impurities such as iron oxide behind as “red mud.” The purified oxide is then dissolved in molten cryolite so that electricity can pull out this element.
tossups.r: That ore is bauxite. For 10 points, name this light metal with atomic number 13, used in airplanes.

tossups.p: This element’s main ore is named for Les Baux-de-Provence [“lay BOH duh proh-VAHNSS”], a village in southern France where Pierre Berthier first described it in 1821. That ore is mined in large amounts in Australia, Guinea, and China.
tossups.r: That ore is bauxite. For 10 points, name this metal, the most abundant metal in Earth’s crust.

tossups.p: Cryolite, a mineral of sodium, fluorine, and this element, was once mined in Greenland, because melted cryolite dissolves this element’s oxide so that electricity can split it. Charles Martin Hall worked out that method in a woodshed lab soon after graduating from Oberlin College.
tossups.r: Hall helped found the company that became Alcoa. For 10 points, name this metal with atomic number 13.

tossups.p: Unlike iron, this metal does not keep crumbling away as it corrodes, because a thin, tough layer of its oxide quickly forms on its surface and seals it off from the air. Anodizing thickens that protective layer using electricity and lets it be dyed bright colors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lightweight metal used to make soda cans, kitchen foil, and airplane bodies.

tossups.p: Rubies and sapphires are colored varieties of corundum [“kuh-RUN-dum”], a mineral made of this element’s oxide that ranks 9 on the Mohs hardness scale. Because it is so hard, ground-up corundum is used as an abrasive in sandpaper and grinding wheels.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this metal with atomic number 13, which British English spells with an extra “i.”

tossups.p: In the thermite reaction, powder of this metal pulls oxygen away from iron(III) oxide, releasing so much heat that molten iron forms and can be used to weld railroad tracks together. This metal also reacts with hydrochloric acid to give off hydrogen gas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, the most abundant metal in Earth’s crust, used to make foil and cans.

tossups.p: Because of a “diagonal relationship” on the periodic table, beryllium behaves much like this element, partly because the two have nearly equal electronegativities. Gallium, indium, and thallium sit below this element in its group. Like boron, this element has three valence electrons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 13, a light metal used to build airplanes.

tossups.p: This element’s hydroxide, which reacts with both acids and bases, is used in some antacid tablets to neutralize stomach acid. A sulfate of this element called alum helps clear cloudy water by making tiny particles clump together so they settle out.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this metal with atomic number 13, which is used in soda cans and foil.

tossups.p: Smelters that make this metal use so much electricity that many are built where power is cheap, such as Iceland, which runs them on hydroelectric and geothermal energy. Recycling this metal saves about 95 percent of the energy needed to make it from ore.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 13, which is recycled from used soda cans and foil.

tossups.p: Tarnished silver turns shiny again when it touches a sheet of this metal in hot water with baking soda, because this metal gives up electrons that turn black silver sulfide back into silver. Alnico magnets are named for this metal, nickel, and cobalt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this metal, the most abundant metal in Earth’s crust, which is refined from bauxite.

clues.t: Element 13, a light, silvery metal just below boron on the periodic table
Used in soda cans, kitchen foil, and airplane bodies
The most abundant metal in Earth’s crust, and the third most abundant element there after oxygen and silicon
Its main ore is bauxite
British English spells its name with an extra “i”
Hall–Héroult process (1886): electricity splits its oxide dissolved in molten cryolite
A thin, tough layer of its oxide keeps it from corroding; anodizing makes that layer thicker
A 100-ounce pyramid of it was set atop the Washington Monument in 1884, when it cost about as much as silver
Thermite: its powder plus iron(III) oxide makes molten iron, used to weld railroad tracks
Recycling it saves about 95 percent of the energy needed to make new metal from ore
About one-third as dense as steel
Humphry Davy named it after alum, a salt used in dyeing
So reactive that it is almost never found as a pure metal in nature
Corundum, its crystallized oxide, ranks 9 on the Mohs scale; rubies and sapphires are colored corundum
Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult were both born in 1863 and both died in 1914
Hall worked out his method in a woodshed lab after graduating from Oberlin College, then helped found the company that became Alcoa
Hans Christian Ørsted made an impure sample in 1825; Friedrich Wöhler made a purer one in 1827
A popular story says Napoleon III gave his most honored guests cutlery made of it; he backed Henri Sainte-Claire Deville’s cheaper method
The Bayer process dissolves its oxide out of bauxite with hot sodium hydroxide, leaving “red mud”
Bauxite is named for Les Baux-de-Provence, France, where Pierre Berthier described it in 1821
Cryolite, a mineral of sodium, fluorine, and this metal, was once mined in Greenland
Mendeleev predicted gallium, the element below it, and named it with the prefix “eka-” plus this element’s name
Its oxide and hydroxide are amphoteric, reacting with both acids and bases; the hydroxide is used in antacids
Alum, a sulfate containing it, makes tiny particles clump together to clear cloudy water
It and beryllium share a diagonal relationship, with nearly equal electronegativities
Its smelters use huge amounts of electricity, so many are built where power is cheap, such as Iceland
It cleans tarnished silver in hot water with baking soda by giving up electrons; alnico magnets contain it, nickel, and cobalt

trap.title: The metal, not its oxide
trap.body: Many clues describe aluminum’s oxide (alumina, corundum, rubies, and sapphires) or its ore (bauxite), and players blurt those names instead of the element. “Aluminium,” the British spelling, is fine, but “alumina” sounds almost the same and is wrong: it means aluminum oxide. Boron, directly above it, and gallium, directly below it, share some of its clues.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this element” or “this metal,” say aluminum (or aluminium). Bauxite is “this ore,” alumina is “this oxide,” and Hall–Héroult is “this process.” Element 5 is boron; element 31 is gallium.
trap.line: Real answer line: Aluminum (or aluminium; accept Al; do not accept “alumina” or “aluminum oxide”)

topics.name: Activation energy
topics.kicker: The energy hill a reaction must climb · Why a match needs a strike
topics.briefing: Wood and paper don’t burst into flames on their own, even though burning releases lots of energy. That’s because a reaction must first get over an energy “hill” called the activation energy. Striking a match supplies that push, and catalysts such as enzymes lower the hill so reactions run faster; Svante Arrhenius introduced the idea in 1889 to explain why heat speeds reactions up.
topics.answerHtml: Activation energy (or Ea; accept energy of activation; prompt on energy barrier; do not accept “catalyst” or “transition state”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On an Arrhenius [“ar-RAY-nee-us”] plot, the natural logarithm of the rate constant is graphed against one over the absolute temperature, giving a straight line whose slope equals the negative of this quantity divided by the gas constant. Chemists use that plot to measure this quantity from experiments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this minimum amount of energy that reactants need in order to react, which catalysts lower.

tossups.p: Henry Eyring’s [“EYE-ring”] transition state theory, published in 1935, relates a reaction’s speed to this quantity and to the short-lived, high-energy arrangement of atoms that forms partway through the reaction. That arrangement sits at the very top of the hump on a reaction’s energy diagram.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy barrier that must be overcome for a reaction to occur, which catalysts lower.

tossups.p: For a simple one-step reaction, this quantity for the reverse reaction equals this quantity for the forward reaction minus the enthalpy change. As a result, an exothermic reaction has a larger value of this quantity when it runs backward, because its products sit lower on the energy diagram.
tossups.r: This quantity is the height of the hump on that diagram. For 10 points, name this energy barrier that reactants must overcome.

tossups.p: Diamond is actually less stable than graphite, but diamonds don’t turn into graphite at room temperature because this quantity for that change is enormous. Chemists call substances like diamond kinetically stable, because they react extremely slowly even when the reaction would release energy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy barrier that must be overcome before a reaction can start.

tossups.p: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann graph of molecular energies, the area under the curve to the right of this quantity shows the fraction of molecules with enough energy to react. Raising the temperature stretches that curve toward higher energies, so a larger fraction of collisions can succeed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this minimum energy needed for a reaction to happen, which a catalyst lowers.

tossups.p: The thermite reaction releases a huge amount of heat, but it needs so much of this quantity to get started that a burning strip of magnesium ribbon is often used to light it. Paper and wood can sit in air for years without catching fire for a similar reason.
tossups.r: Striking a match supplies this quantity. For 10 points, name this minimum energy needed to start a reaction.

tossups.p: In the Arrhenius [“ar-RAY-nee-us”] equation, a reaction’s rate constant depends on the temperature, a frequency factor called A, and this quantity. Reactions with a larger value of this quantity run more slowly and speed up more sharply when heated.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy barrier, the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur.

tossups.p: In a reaction with several steps, each step has its own value of this quantity, drawn as a separate hump on the energy diagram, and the step with the largest value is usually the slowest, rate-determining step. The valleys between those humps stand for reaction intermediates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy barrier that reactants must climb over, which catalysts and enzymes lower.

tossups.p: A sugar cube sitting in air does not burn, even though its reaction with oxygen releases a lot of energy, because this quantity for that reaction is high. In cells, the same overall reaction happens at body temperature in many small steps, each with a much smaller value of this quantity.
tossups.r: Enzymes lower this quantity. For 10 points, name this energy barrier that must be overcome for a reaction to begin.

tossups.p: A rule of thumb says that many reactions near room temperature roughly double in speed for every 10-degree Celsius rise, a result that follows from typical sizes of this quantity. Cooking food at a higher temperature speeds up its chemical reactions for the same reason.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur, which enzymes lower.

tossups.p: In an endothermic reaction, this quantity must be at least as large as the reaction’s enthalpy change, because the products sit higher on the energy diagram than the reactants. On that diagram, this quantity is measured from the reactants up to the transition state.
tossups.r: Catalysts lower this quantity without changing the enthalpy change. For 10 points, name this energy barrier for a reaction.

tossups.p: According to collision theory, colliding molecules react only if they are lined up in the right orientation and their collision energy exceeds this quantity. Crushing a solid into powder speeds up a reaction by causing more collisions, but it does not change this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this minimum energy needed for a reaction, which catalysts lower by providing a different pathway.

tossups.p: Svante Arrhenius [“ar-RAY-nee-us”], who won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how salts break apart into ions, introduced this quantity in 1889 to explain why heating speeds up reactions. This quantity is usually measured in kilojoules per mole.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy barrier, the minimum energy reactants need to react.

tossups.p: A glow stick placed in a freezer glows more dimly but lasts much longer, because at low temperatures fewer molecules have enough energy to get over this barrier. For the same reason, milk spoils more slowly in a refrigerator.
tossups.r: A match needs a strike to supply this quantity. For 10 points, name this minimum energy that reactants need to get a reaction going.

tossups.p: A mixture of hydrogen and chlorine gases can sit safely in the dark, but bright light can set it off, because light splits a few chlorine molecules and helps the reaction get over this barrier. Robert Bunsen and Henry Roscoe used that reaction to measure the brightness of light.
tossups.r: Catalysts such as enzymes lower this barrier. For 10 points, name this minimum energy needed to start a reaction.

clues.t: The minimum energy reactants need for a reaction to start
Catalysts, including enzymes, speed up reactions by lowering it
Striking a match supplies it, which is why matches don’t light by themselves in the box
Pictured as a hill or barrier that reactants must climb before they can become products
On an energy diagram, it is the height of the hump from the reactants up to the peak
The top of the hump is the transition state, also called the activated complex
Svante Arrhenius introduced the idea in 1889 to explain why heating speeds up reactions
The Arrhenius equation links a rate constant to the temperature, a frequency factor A, and this quantity
Heating speeds up reactions because more molecules have at least this much energy
Collision theory: molecules react only if they collide in the right orientation with enough energy; crushing a solid speeds collisions but doesn’t change it
Usually measured in kilojoules per mole
A catalyst lowers it but doesn’t change the reaction’s overall enthalpy change
On a Maxwell–Boltzmann graph, the area to the right of it shows the fraction of molecules with enough energy to react
An Arrhenius plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line whose slope is minus this quantity divided by the gas constant
For the reverse of a one-step reaction, it equals the forward value minus the enthalpy change, so exothermic reactions have a bigger value backward
Diamond is less stable than graphite but doesn’t turn into graphite, because this barrier is enormous (kinetic stability)
Henry Eyring’s transition state theory (1935) relates reaction speed to it and to the transition state
Thermite needs so much of it that a burning magnesium ribbon is often used to start it
Rule of thumb: many reactions roughly double in speed for every 10 °C rise, because of typical values of it
In a multistep reaction, the step with the biggest hump is usually the slowest, rate-determining step
In an endothermic reaction, it must be at least as large as the enthalpy change
A sugar cube doesn’t burn in air because this barrier is high; cells break sugar down in small, enzyme-assisted steps
A glow stick in a freezer lasts longer because fewer molecules can get over this barrier when cold
Light helps a hydrogen–chlorine mixture get over this barrier and explode; Bunsen and Roscoe used that reaction to measure light

trap.title: The barrier, not the helper
trap.body: Catalysts and enzymes work by lowering activation energy, so clues about one sound like clues about the other. Players also mix it up with the transition state, which is the arrangement of atoms at the top of the hump, and with the enthalpy change, which is the overall energy difference between reactants and products.
trap.fix: Listen for the question word. “This quantity,” “this energy,” or “this barrier,” measured in kilojoules per mole, means activation energy; “these substances” that are not used up means catalysts. The peak itself is the transition state, and reactants versus products is the enthalpy change.
trap.line: Real answer line: Activation energy (or Ea; accept energy of activation; prompt on energy barrier; do not accept “catalyst” or “transition state”)
